0.title: Habakkuk: The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
0.overview:
Habakkuk is the book for anyone who has looked at the world and wanted to argue with God. Most prophets carry God's message to the people. Habakkuk carries the people's questions to God, and writes down both sides of the conversation. It begins with a complaint and ends with a song.

We know nothing about him beyond his name. He preached in the last years of the seventh century BC, shortly before the Babylonians began to carry Judah away (2 Kgs 24:1). Josiah's reforms had come and gone, the nation had slid back into corruption, and a new superpower was rising in the east.

The book has three movements. Chapter 1 is a dialogue. Habakkuk asks why God does nothing about the violence and broken courts in Judah: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (1:2). God replies that he is doing something: I am raising up the Chaldeans (1:6), the Babylonians. That answer is harder than the question, and the prophet comes straight back with a bigger one. How can God, who is of purer eyes than to see evil, use a nation even worse than the one he is punishing? (1:13).

Chapter 2 is God's answer. Habakkuk climbs his watchtower to wait for it, and God tells him to write the vision plainly, because it has an appointed time: If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay (2:3). Then comes the sentence that the whole Bible builds on: the righteous shall live by his faith (2:4). The rest of the chapter is a taunt song of five woes over the proud conqueror, ending with a line of great stillness: But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (2:20).

Chapter 3 is a prayer set to music. Habakkuk remembers how God came to rescue his people at the exodus, trembles at what is coming, and then says the words the book is famous for: Though the fig tree should not blossom, and every crop and flock fails, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation (3:17-18).

Notice what Habakkuk is never given. He never receives a full explanation of why God uses violent nations, or why the wicked prosper while the righteous suffer. What he is given is a promise, a command to wait, and God himself. That is usually what we are given too.

The turning point is 2:4, and its influence is hard to overstate. Paul quotes it in Romans to show that God puts sinners right with himself through faith in Christ and not by their own performance (Rom 1:17). He quotes it again in Galatians against those who wanted to add law-keeping to the gospel (Gal 3:11). Hebrews quotes it to keep frightened Christians from shrinking back (Heb 10:38). It was through Paul's use of this verse that Martin Luther came to peace with God, and the doctrine of justification by faith alone was recovered for the church. (The ESV notes that the word may also be rendered "faithfulness"; these notes explain both readings.)

Habakkuk points to Christ in several ways. The vision that will surely come is applied by Hebrews to the return of Jesus: Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay (Heb 10:37). The cup of judgment that comes round to the oppressor (2:16) is the cup Christ drank for his people. And when God marches out for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed, crushing the head of the wicked (3:13), we are back at the promise of Eden, fulfilled at the cross.

Above all, this little book teaches us how to live when God's timing is not ours. Bring him the real question, and do not dress it up. Wait for his answer, and be willing to be corrected by it. Trust the promise you have been given rather than the evidence you can see. And learn to put your joy where nothing can reach it, so that when the fields are bare you can still say yet I will rejoice in the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — How Long Shall I Cry for Help?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Habakkuk begins not with a message to the people but with a protest to God: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (v. 2). He sees Destruction and violence, and a legal system where the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: God allows his people to bring him their hardest questions, and a prophet's honest protest is part of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.

Habakkuk's name appears nowhere else in Scripture; this book is all we have of him, and it is built differently from the others. The traffic runs the other way. Other prophets stand between God and the people carrying God's word down to them; this man stands in the same place carrying the people's questions up, and then writes down what God says back.

The date is fixed by what he expects. Babylon has not arrived yet, but is coming (v. 6; 2 Kgs 24:1); Josiah's reforms are behind him, and the corruption of verses 2-4 is back. He is preaching in the last years before the deportations begin.

Notice too what he is not doing. He is not writing a treatise about suffering. He is praying, and the prayer is preserved in Scripture so that we may pray like it.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you "Violence!" and you will not save? Why do you make me see iniquity, and why do you idly look at wrong? Destruction and violence are before me; strife and contention arise. So the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth. For the wicked surround the righteous; so justice goes forth perverted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you "Violence!" and you will not save?

The first words of the book are a complaint. How long is the standard cry of the psalms in the dark: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps 13:1). Even in heaven the martyrs cry how long (Rev 6:10).

Two things are striking here. First, Habakkuk says God is not listening: you will not hear. He prays it straight to God's face. Second, he does it as a believer. He does not walk away; he takes his complaint to the only one who can do anything about it. That is the difference between unbelief and honest faith.

Why do you make me see iniquity, and why do you idly look at wrong? Destruction and violence are before me; strife and contention arise.

So the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth. For the wicked surround the righteous; so justice goes forth perverted.

Now the detail of the complaint, and it is about his own country. Destruction and violence in the streets. The law is paralyzed: the courts exist, the statutes are on the books, and nothing happens. Justice, when it finally moves, comes out bent: justice goes forth perverted.

Anyone who has watched a corrupt system up close knows the feeling. And notice the sharpest part of the protest: why do you idly look at wrong? The problem is not that God cannot see. It is that he seems to be watching and doing nothing.

Scripture is not embarrassed by this prayer. It is in the Bible, which means God is not offended by his children asking why. But notice also what Habakkuk does next: he waits for an answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — I Am Raising Up the Chaldeans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers, and the answer is worse than the question: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told (v. 5). He is raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, swifter than leopards, who gather captives like sand and laugh at every fortress (vv. 6-10) — guilty men, whose own might is their god! (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God rules the rise of empires, and his answers to prayer are often harder than we expected.

verseByVerse.quote: "Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astounded. For I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told. For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, who march through the breadth of the earth, to seize dwellings not their own. They are dreaded and fearsome; their justice and dignity go forth from themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astounded. For I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told.

God answers. He is at work after all, and the work is so surprising that Habakkuk would not believe it if he were simply told. Paul quoted this verse when some in a synagogue refused the gospel, warning them not to be scoffers who miss what God is doing (Acts 13:41).

For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, who march through the breadth of the earth, to seize dwellings not their own.

Here is the answer, and it lands like a blow. The Chaldeans are the Babylonians, the rising superpower. God's response to injustice in Judah is to bring in an army far more violent than anything in Jerusalem.

Notice who is acting: I am raising up the Chaldeans. God does not merely permit Babylon; he raises them up. Jeremiah, preaching at the same time, even calls Nebuchadnezzar God's servant (Jer 25:9), meaning a tool in his hand. God governs the nations that do not know him, and uses them without approving of them. Verse 11 will call these same men guilty.

They are dreaded and fearsome; their justice and dignity go forth from themselves.

They are dreaded and fearsome, and their justice and dignity go forth from themselves: they make their own rules and answer to nobody. That is the mark of every tyranny, ancient or modern.

The lesson runs beyond Babylon. If God can raise up an empire, he can raise up, or remove, a government, an employer or a diagnosis. That truth is terrifying if God is only powerful, and steadying if he is also good.

verseByVerse.quote: Their horses are swifter than leopards, more fierce than the evening wolves; their horsemen press proudly on. Their horsemen come from afar; they fly like an eagle swift to devour. They all come for violence, all their faces forward. They gather captives like sand. At kings they scoff, and at rulers they laugh. They laugh at every fortress, for they pile up earth and take it. Then they sweep by like the wind and go on, guilty men, whose own might is their god!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their horses are swifter than leopards, more fierce than the evening wolves; their horsemen press proudly on. Their horsemen come from afar; they fly like an eagle swift to devour.

A portrait of a war machine. Their cavalry is faster than leopards and hungrier than the evening wolves, the ones that hunt at dusk, and they come on like an eagle swift to devour.

They all come for violence, all their faces forward. They gather captives like sand.

At kings they scoff, and at rulers they laugh. They laugh at every fortress, for they pile up earth and take it.

They collect people like sand, uncountable and worthless to them. Kings and fortresses are a joke; they simply build an earth ramp up to the wall and walk in.

Then they sweep by like the wind and go on, guilty men, whose own might is their god!"

And there is God's own verdict on the army he is sending: guilty men, whose own might is their god. Babylon is not innocent, and their turn will come in chapter 2. But God can use a guilty nation to discipline his own people without excusing either.

This is a hard doctrine, and a comforting one. Nothing in history is out of control. But it means God's answers to our prayers sometimes come in a shape we would never have chosen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Why Do You Idly Look?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet comes back: Are you not from everlasting, O LORD my God, my Holy One? We shall not die (v. 12). But how can one of purer eyes than to see evil stay silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? (v. 13). The conqueror hauls up whole nations like fish in a net and worships the net that made him rich (vv. 14-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Faith argues with God on the basis of who God is, and refuses to accept that cruelty has the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you not from everlasting, O LORD my God, my Holy One? We shall not die. O LORD, you have ordained them as a judgment, and you, O Rock, have established them for reproof. You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? You make mankind like the fish of the sea, like crawling things that have no ruler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you not from everlasting, O LORD my God, my Holy One? We shall not die. O LORD, you have ordained them as a judgment, and you, O Rock, have established them for reproof.

Habakkuk answers God, and watch how he does it. He does not start with his objection; he starts with who God is. Are you not from everlasting? My God, my Holy One, O Rock. He is reasoning from God's character to his confusion, not the other way round.

In the middle comes a statement of faith that carries the whole book: We shall not die. Whatever this invasion means, it cannot mean the end of God's people, because God has promised otherwise.

And he accepts the Babylonians as God's instrument: you have ordained them as a judgment. Habakkuk is not fighting the doctrine of God's sovereignty. He is struggling with something else.

You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he?

Here is the real question of the book, and it is sharper than the first one. Habakkuk believes two things that seem impossible together. God is of purer eyes than to see evil: he is utterly holy. And God is using a nation far worse than Judah to punish Judah. How can a holy God remain silent while the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he?

Every believer meets this question in some form. Not "why is there suffering?" in the abstract, but "why do the people who trample others seem to prosper, while those who try to do right are trodden down?" Asaph asked it in Psalm 73 and said it wore him out until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end (Ps 73:17).

You make mankind like the fish of the sea, like crawling things that have no ruler.

The complaint gets bleaker. People are being treated like fish, or like insects with no one to protect them. That is what conquest does: it reduces human beings made in God's image to a catch.

verseByVerse.quote: He brings all of them up with a hook; he drags them out with his net; he gathers them in his dragnet; so he rejoices and is glad. Therefore he sacrifices to his net and makes offerings to his dragnet; for by them he lives in luxury, and his food is rich. Is he then to keep on emptying his net and mercilessly killing nations forever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brings all of them up with a hook; he drags them out with his net; he gathers them in his dragnet; so he rejoices and is glad.

Therefore he sacrifices to his net and makes offerings to his dragnet; for by them he lives in luxury, and his food is rich.

The picture is developed with painful precision. The conqueror (the ESV notes the He is the wicked foe) hauls nations in with hook, net and dragnet, and the harvest makes him glad. Then comes the detail that says everything about him: he sacrifices to his net.

He worships his own equipment. Babylon's religion was, in the end, admiration of Babylon's methods: the army, the siege ramps, the machinery of empire. (The ESV notes the Hebrew of the next line reads "his portion is fat": the net keeps him in luxury.)

Every generation sacrifices to its net. A business can worship its own model, a country its military or its economy, a person his own competence and hard work. The test is simple: what do we thank when things go well?

Is he then to keep on emptying his net and mercilessly killing nations forever?

The chapter ends on the unanswered question: is this how it will always be? Forever?

Habakkuk stops there and, in the next chapter, climbs his watchtower to wait for God's reply. That is the right instinct when our questions have run out. We are not told to pretend we have answers. We are told to take our stand and wait for the God who answers.

1.title: O LORD, How Long?
1.overview:
The oracle Habakkuk saw opens with a protest: how long must he cry for help while God does not hear or save? He sees iniquity, destruction, violence, strife and contention; the law is paralyzed and justice comes out perverted because the wicked surround the righteous (vv. 1-4).

God answers that he is doing a work his prophet would not believe if told: he is raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and hasty nation who seize homes not their own, dreaded and self-justifying, with horses swifter than leopards, gathering captives like sand, laughing at kings and fortresses and piling up earth to take them — guilty men whose own might is their god (vv. 5-11).

Habakkuk replies by appealing to God's eternity and holiness: "Are you not from everlasting ... We shall not die", acknowledging that God has ordained this nation for judgment. But how can one of purer eyes than to see evil remain silent while the wicked swallows up one more righteous than he? People are treated like fish caught with hook and dragnet by a conqueror who sacrifices to his net and lives in luxury. Is he to keep emptying his net and killing nations forever? (vv. 12-17).
1.theology:
God welcomes the honest protest of faith; lament belongs in Scripture and in prayer (vv. 2-4; Ps 13:1; Rev 6:10).

God is at work even when he appears idle, and his work may be beyond what we would believe (v. 5; Acts 13:41).

God raises up and rules nations that do not know him, using them without excusing them (vv. 6, 11; Jer 25:9).

Faith reasons from God's character to its confusion, not from its confusion to doubt about God (v. 12).

The hardest problem is not suffering in general but the prospering of the violent, and Scripture takes the question seriously (v. 13; Ps 73:16-17).

People who succeed by force end by worshipping their own methods (v. 16).

When our questions run out, the right response is to take our stand and wait for God to answer (v. 17; 2:1).
1.examples:
A prophet who takes the people's questions to God instead of God's answers to the people.

Courts that are open, laws that are on the books, and justice that never arrives.

An answer to prayer that is harder than the problem.

Cavalry faster than leopards and hungrier than wolves at dusk.

Prisoners counted like grains of sand.

A conqueror burning incense to his own fishing net.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will take my stand at my watchpost, says the prophet, waiting for God's reply (v. 1). God answers: Write the vision; make it plain on tablets, so he may run who reads it (v. 2), for though it seems slow, it will surely come; it will not delay (v. 3). Then the heart of the book: the proud soul is puffed up, but the righteous shall live by his faith (v. 4), while the conqueror's greed is as wide as Sheol (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to the delay of justice is a promise to be trusted, and the righteous live by trusting it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will take my stand at my watchpost and station myself on the tower, and look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint. And the LORD answered me: "Write the vision; make it plain on tablets, so he may run who reads it. For still the vision awaits its appointed time; it hastens to the end—it will not lie. If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will take my stand at my watchpost and station myself on the tower, and look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint.

Habakkuk has fired his questions. Now he does what few of us do: he waits for the answer. He pictures himself as a watchman on the city wall, scanning the horizon.

Two things here are simple enough to copy today. He expects God to speak, and he expects to be corrected: what I will answer concerning my complaint. He knows that God's reply may show him that his complaint was wrong. Honest prayer includes the willingness to be answered.

And the LORD answered me: "Write the vision; make it plain on tablets, so he may run who reads it.

God does answer. And the first instruction is to write it down, plain on tablets, in letters large enough that he may run who reads it: a message legible at a glance, like a notice on a wall, so that anyone hurrying past can take it in and carry it away.

This is why we have a Bible. God's answers are not private impressions but written words, given so that they can be read, remembered and passed on long after the prophet is dead.

For still the vision awaits its appointed time; it hastens to the end—it will not lie. If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay.

Here is God's answer to the question of delay. The vision has an appointed time: God has a date for it, and the date is fixed. It will not lie: it is not an empty comfort.

Then the phrase that has steadied believers ever since: If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay. Notice the honesty of if it seems slow. God does not pretend that waiting is easy or that his timing feels quick to us. He says that what looks like slowness from below is exactness from above.

The writer to the Hebrews quotes this verse to a church tempted to give up under pressure, and applies it to the return of Christ: Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay (Heb 10:37). The final answer to every unanswered prayer is a person, and he is on his way.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith. "Moreover, wine is a traitor, an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough. He gathers for himself all nations and collects as his own all peoples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith.

This is the verse the whole book turns on, and one of the most important sentences in the Bible.

Two kinds of people are set side by side. The first is the proud man, here the Babylonian conqueror: his soul is puffed up, swollen with himself, and it is not upright within him. Everything he has is held by force, and it will not last.

The second is the righteous, and his whole life is described in one phrase: shall live by his faith. He does not live by explanations, because Habakkuk has not been given many. He does not live by visible evidence, because the evidence at the moment is an approaching army. He lives by trusting the God who has spoken.

The ESV notes that the word may be translated "faithfulness". Some read it that way: the righteous person lives by being steady and loyal to God. That is true in itself, and Habakkuk will model it in chapter 3. But the Reformed tradition, following the way the New Testament uses the verse, reads it as faith, trust in God rather than in ourselves, and the context supports that: the contrast is with a man puffed up with self-reliance. Faith and faithfulness are not opposites in any case; real trust keeps trusting.

The New Testament quotes this line three times, and each use matters. Paul writes, The righteous shall live by faith, and builds on it his gospel that God justifies sinners through faith in Christ, not by works (Rom 1:17). He quotes it again against those who wanted to add the law to the gospel: no one is justified before God by the law (Gal 3:11). And Hebrews uses it to keep struggling Christians from shrinking back (Heb 10:38).

It is also the verse that stands behind the Reformation. Martin Luther, agonising over how a sinner could ever be right with God, found the answer through Paul's use of these words in Romans, and the doctrine of justification by faith alone came back to the church with him.

So the answer God gives to a prophet who cannot understand his times is not a full explanation. It is an invitation: trust me, and you will live.

"Moreover, wine is a traitor, an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough. He gathers for himself all nations and collects as his own all peoples."

Now the proud man is described further. (The ESV notes that where the Hebrew text has wine, a Dead Sea Scroll reads "wealth", and that the meaning of these two lines is uncertain.) Either way the portrait is clear: a man drunk on success, never at rest, whose appetite is as wide as Sheol, the grave that never fills.

That is a perfect description of greed. It does not stop when it has enough, because it never has enough. And it is the exact opposite of the quiet life of faith in verse 4.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Woe to the Plunderer and the Builder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plundered nations take up a taunt: Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own, for his debtors will rise and plunder him (vv. 6-8). Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high — the very stones of the house will testify against him (vv. 9-11). Woe to him who builds a town with blood: such labour is only fuel for fire, For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Wealth and security built on other people collapse, while God's glory is what finally fills the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall not all these take up their taunt against him, with scoffing and riddles for him, and say, "Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own— for how long?— and loads himself with pledges!" Will not your debtors suddenly arise, and those awake who will make you tremble? Then you will be spoil for them. Because you have plundered many nations, all the remnant of the peoples shall plunder you, for the blood of man and violence to the earth, to cities and all who dwell in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall not all these take up their taunt against him, with scoffing and riddles for him, and say, "Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own— for how long?— and loads himself with pledges!"

Now come five woes, sung by the nations Babylon has swallowed. It is a bitter, mocking song, and each verse begins the same way.

The first woe is against plunder: Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own. The word pledges is the language of debt. Babylon has taken from everyone, as a ruthless lender collects security from the poor. And the taunt asks the question Habakkuk asked: for how long?

Will not your debtors suddenly arise, and those awake who will make you tremble? Then you will be spoil for them.

Because you have plundered many nations, all the remnant of the peoples shall plunder you, for the blood of man and violence to the earth, to cities and all who dwell in them.

The answer is that the debts will be called in. Those who were robbed will suddenly arise, and the plunderer becomes the spoil. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC, and the wealth of the world changed hands again.

Underneath the politics is a moral principle: for the blood of man and violence to the earth. God keeps account of blood. The phrase is repeated in verse 17, framing the whole song.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high, to be safe from the reach of harm! You have devised shame for your house by cutting off many peoples; you have forfeited your life. For the stone will cry out from the wall, and the beam from the woodwork respond.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high, to be safe from the reach of harm!

The second woe is against security bought with other people's suffering. The picture is an eagle's nest on high, out of reach of predators. That is what the money is for: safety. Fortified palaces, walls, an estate the trouble cannot reach.

It is a thoroughly modern woe. Much of what people accumulate is an attempt to build a nest where harm cannot come: enough savings, enough insurance, enough distance from the neighbourhoods where things go wrong. The impulse is understandable. The illusion is that it works.

You have devised shame for your house by cutting off many peoples; you have forfeited your life.

For the stone will cry out from the wall, and the beam from the woodwork respond.

The house built to protect the family has brought shame on it instead, and the man who schemed for his life has forfeited it.

Then a haunting image: the building itself gives evidence. The stone will cry out from the wall, and the beam from the woodwork respond, as one witness answers another in court. Every stone was paid for by somebody. In God's courtroom the walls can testify.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who builds a town with blood and founds a city on iniquity! Behold, is it not from the LORD of hosts that peoples labor merely for fire, and nations weary themselves for nothing? For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to him who builds a town with blood and founds a city on iniquity!

The third woe is against public grandeur built on human cost. Babylon was famous for its building projects, raised by armies of prisoners and slave labour. Micah said the same of Jerusalem in his day: they build Zion with blood (Mic 3:10).

Behold, is it not from the LORD of hosts that peoples labor merely for fire, and nations weary themselves for nothing?

All that work, and it ends as fuel: peoples labor merely for fire. Not because effort is meaningless in itself, but because God has decreed that what is built on injustice will burn. The magnificent city became, in time, a mound of ruins in the desert.

For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

And then, in the middle of five woes, this. It is one of the great promises of the Bible. Empires rise and burn; what finally fills the world is not their glory but God's, and the filling is total, as the waters cover the sea: not puddles here and there, but depth everywhere.

Isaiah made the same promise about the reign of the shoot from Jesse (Isa 11:9). This is where history is going. Every believer who works at something small and good is working with the grain of that future, and every empire built on blood is working against it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — Woe to the Degrader and the Idolater
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink in order to shame them: the cup will come round to him (vv. 15-17). And woe to the idol-maker who says to wood, Awake, for there is no breath at all in it (vv. 18-19). Against all of it stands one quiet line: But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who degrade others drink their own cup, and the idols people trust cannot speak; only the living God is to be feared.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink— you pour out your wrath and make them drunk, in order to gaze at their nakedness! You will have your fill of shame instead of glory. Drink, yourself, and show your uncircumcision! The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you, and utter shame will come upon your glory! The violence done to Lebanon will overwhelm you, as will the destruction of the beasts that terrified them, for the blood of man and violence to the earth, to cities and all who dwell in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink— you pour out your wrath and make them drunk, in order to gaze at their nakedness!

The fourth woe is against deliberate degradation. The picture is of a man who gets his neighbour drunk in order to humiliate him and enjoy the spectacle. Conquering armies did this literally; Babylon did it to whole nations, stripping them of dignity for the pleasure of watching.

There is a version of this in every age: the humiliation of a colleague for entertainment, the exposure of someone's shame online for an audience. God calls it a woe.

You will have your fill of shame instead of glory. Drink, yourself, and show your uncircumcision! The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you, and utter shame will come upon your glory!

The sentence fits the crime: Drink, yourself. The cup passes around the table, and it reaches Babylon at last. The cup in the LORD's right hand is the prophets' picture of his judgment, which Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink (Jer 25:15-17).

Christians cannot read about that cup without remembering Gethsemane, where Jesus prayed about a cup he did not deserve and drank it anyway. The only people who never drink this cup are those whose cup he took.

The violence done to Lebanon will overwhelm you, as will the destruction of the beasts that terrified them, for the blood of man and violence to the earth, to cities and all who dwell in them.

Babylon stripped the famous cedar forests of Lebanon for its building projects and hunted the wildlife. God notices that too. The charge repeats the refrain of verse 8: for the blood of man and violence to the earth. Cruelty to people and destruction of the land are named in one breath.

verseByVerse.quote: "What profit is an idol when its maker has shaped it, a metal image, a teacher of lies? For its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols! Woe to him who says to a wooden thing, Awake; to a silent stone, Arise! Can this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"What profit is an idol when its maker has shaped it, a metal image, a teacher of lies? For its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols!

The fifth woe reaches the root of all the others: idolatry. The logic is devastating in its simplicity. The man shaped the thing himself, and now he trusts in his own creation. He is, in the end, trusting himself and calling it religion.

An idol is a teacher of lies because it promises what it cannot give. Modern idols do not usually have faces; they are the career, the family name, the political cause, the pension. What they have in common with the ancient kind is that we made them, and they cannot save us.

Woe to him who says to a wooden thing, Awake; to a silent stone, Arise! Can this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it.

Picture the scene the prophet paints: a man standing in front of a carved block shouting Awake, and nothing happens. The gold plating is beautiful. There is no breath at all in it.

But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him."

And then the chapter ends with a sentence of extraordinary calm. After the roaring of armies, the boasting of the proud and the shouting at wooden gods: But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.

He has not left his throne. He is not asleep, or absent, or unaware. The right response is not more noise but silence, the hush of a courtroom when the judge enters.

Habakkuk began the book shouting questions at heaven. He will end it singing. This verse is the turning point between the two, and it is where every believer who has been arguing with God eventually has to stand: not with all the answers, but quiet before the God who has them.

2.title: The Righteous Shall Live by His Faith
2.overview:
Habakkuk takes his stand at his watchpost to see what God will say and what he will answer concerning his complaint (v. 1). God tells him to write the vision plainly on tablets so that a runner can read it; the vision awaits its appointed time and will not lie, and though it seems slow it will surely come (vv. 2-3). The proud man's soul is puffed up and not upright, but the righteous shall live by his faith; the greedy conqueror is never at rest, his appetite as wide as Sheol (vv. 4-5).

The plundered nations take up five woes against him. Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own, for his debtors will arise and plunder him for the blood of man and violence to the earth (vv. 6-8). Woe to him who gets evil gain to set his nest on high, for the stone will cry out from the wall (vv. 9-11). Woe to him who builds a town with blood: peoples labour merely for fire, while the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (vv. 12-14).

Woe to him who makes his neighbours drunk to gaze at their shame, for the cup in the LORD's right hand will come round to him, and the violence done to Lebanon will overwhelm him (vv. 15-17). Woe to the maker of idols, who trusts his own creation, shouting "Awake" at wood and stone in which there is no breath. But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (vv. 18-20).
2.theology:
Honest prayer waits for God's answer and is willing to be corrected by it (v. 1).

God gives his answers in writing, so that they can be read, remembered and passed on (v. 2).

God's promises have an appointed time; what looks like slowness from below is exactness from above (v. 3; Heb 10:37).

The righteous live by faith in God rather than by explanations or visible evidence — the verse on which Paul builds justification by faith (v. 4; Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11; Heb 10:38).

Greed is an appetite that can never be filled, the opposite of the quiet life of faith (v. 5).

Wealth, security and grandeur built on other people are repaid in kind, and the very stones bear witness (vv. 6-13).

The earth's future is not the glory of empires but the knowledge of God's glory filling it completely (v. 14; Isa 11:9).

Idols are lies we make and then trust, and the God who is in his holy temple silences every rival (vv. 18-20).
2.examples:
A prophet climbing his tower to wait for a reply.

A message written large enough to read at a run.

Two men side by side: one swollen with himself, one living by trust.

An appetite as wide as the grave, which never fills.

An eagle's nest built high with other people's money.

Stones in a wall giving evidence in court.

A man shouting "Awake!" at a block of gold-plated wood.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet (v. 1): O LORD, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O LORD, do I fear. In the midst of the years revive it ... in wrath remember mercy (v. 2). Then God comes: His splendor covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise (vv. 3-4); plague goes before him, the eternal mountains scatter, and distant peoples tremble (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The right prayer in a dark time is that God would act again as he has acted before, and remember mercy in the middle of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth. O LORD, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O LORD, do I fear. In the midst of the years revive it; in the midst of the years make it known; in wrath remember mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth.

The book ends as a psalm. Shigionoth is a musical direction, like the note at the end of verse 19 about stringed instruments, and the word Selah that appears three times in this chapter is another. This prayer was meant to be sung in public worship.

Pause over that. A man's private wrestling with God became a song for the congregation. The Bible turns honest struggle into worship, which is why so many believers in trouble find their own words in Scripture.

O LORD, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O LORD, do I fear. In the midst of the years revive it; in the midst of the years make it known; in wrath remember mercy.

Habakkuk has heard what God is going to do, and it frightens him: your work, O LORD, do I fear. He is not pretending to be braver than he is.

Then he prays three short petitions to learn by heart. In the midst of the years revive it: do again, in our own time, what you have done before. In the midst of the years make it known: let people see it. And then the loveliest: in wrath remember mercy.

He does not ask God to cancel the judgment. He has accepted that it is just. He asks that, in the middle of it, God would not forget to be merciful. That is a prayer for a nation under discipline, for a church in decline, and for a family reaping what it has sown.

verseByVerse.quote: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah His splendor covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. His brightness was like the light; rays flashed from his hand; and there he veiled his power. Before him went pestilence, and plague followed at his heels. He stood and measured the earth; he looked and shook the nations; then the eternal mountains were scattered; the everlasting hills sank low. His were the everlasting ways. I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction; the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah His splendor covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.

Now the prayer becomes a vision. Habakkuk looks back to the beginning, when God came to his people at Sinai and led them through the wilderness. Teman and Mount Paran are in the desert country to the south, the region of Sinai; Moses used the same geography in his blessing (Deut 33:2).

The prophet is doing what believers should do in the dark: remembering. He cannot see God at work in his own day, so he rehearses what God has already done.

His brightness was like the light; rays flashed from his hand; and there he veiled his power.

A striking line: even this blaze of light is God veiling himself. What we can bear to see is the shielded edge of his glory.

Before him went pestilence, and plague followed at his heels.

Plague and pestilence walk in front of him and behind him (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "feet"), like servants attending a king. The language recalls the plagues of Egypt. Even the forces that terrify us are on a lead in his hand.

He stood and measured the earth; he looked and shook the nations; then the eternal mountains were scattered; the everlasting hills sank low. His were the everlasting ways.

He only has to stand and look, and the nations shake. Notice the contrast in the words: the eternal mountains and everlasting hills turn out not to be everlasting at all, while His were the everlasting ways. Only God is permanent. Everything we call solid is temporary by comparison.

I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction; the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble.

Desert peoples on the route of the exodus shake in their tents as God passes. The point is not their guilt in particular but the sheer effect of God's approach.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Was God angry with the rivers and the sea, or riding on your chariot of salvation? (v. 8). Mountains writhe, the deep lifts its hands, sun and moon stand still at the flash of his arrows (vv. 9-11). He marches for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed, crushing the head of the house of the wicked (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's terrifying power in history is aimed at one thing: the rescue of his people through his anointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Was your wrath against the rivers, O LORD? Was your anger against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you rode on your horses, on your chariot of salvation? You stripped the sheath from your bow, calling for many arrows. Selah You split the earth with rivers. The mountains saw you and writhed; the raging waters swept on; the deep gave forth its voice; it lifted its hands on high. The sun and moon stood still in their place at the light of your arrows as they sped, at the flash of your glittering spear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Was your wrath against the rivers, O LORD? Was your anger against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you rode on your horses, on your chariot of salvation?

A question with a beautiful answer hidden in it. When God split the sea at the exodus and stopped the Jordan, was he angry with the water? Of course not. The rivers were not the target. He was riding on your chariot of salvation: the whole display of power had one purpose, to rescue his people.

That reframes a great deal. The upheavals in our lives are not God losing his temper with the furniture. When he shakes things, he is going somewhere, and the destination is salvation.

You stripped the sheath from your bow, calling for many arrows. Selah You split the earth with rivers.

God unsheathes his bow like a warrior going into battle (the ESV notes the meaning of the line is uncertain in Hebrew). And he split the earth with rivers, as he brought water from the rock in the desert.

The mountains saw you and writhed; the raging waters swept on; the deep gave forth its voice; it lifted its hands on high.

The sun and moon stood still in their place at the light of your arrows as they sped, at the flash of your glittering spear.

Creation responds like a living thing: mountains writhed, the deep gave forth its voice and lifted its hands like a man surrendering. Even the sun and moon stood still, as they did in Joshua's day, because the light of God's arrows outshone them.

verseByVerse.quote: You marched through the earth in fury; you threshed the nations in anger. You went out for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed. You crushed the head of the house of the wicked, laying him bare from thigh to neck. Selah You pierced with his own arrows the heads of his warriors, who came like a whirlwind to scatter me, rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret. You trampled the sea with your horses, the surging of mighty waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You marched through the earth in fury; you threshed the nations in anger.

You went out for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed. You crushed the head of the house of the wicked, laying him bare from thigh to neck. Selah

Here is the centre of the vision, and the word to notice is repeated: salvation, and then salvation again. God's marching and threshing are not random violence. You went out for the salvation of your people.

Your anointed means, in the first place, the king God had chosen to lead his people, and behind him the people themselves. Christians cannot help reading further. The word for God's anointed one is the word Messiah, and the Bible's story runs toward one Anointed through whom God saves.

And notice how the enemy falls: You crushed the head of the house of the wicked (the ESV notes the meaning of the rest of the line is uncertain). Ever since Eden, God's promise has been that the offspring of the woman would bruise the serpent's head (Gen 3:15). Every head-crushing rescue in the Old Testament is an echo of that promise, and it was fulfilled at the cross, where Christ destroyed the one who had the power of death.

You pierced with his own arrows the heads of his warriors, who came like a whirlwind to scatter me, rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret.

You trampled the sea with your horses, the surging of mighty waters.

The enemy is destroyed with his own weapons, and God's horses trample the sea as easily as a field. The men who came rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret discover that the poor have a defender.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Though the Fig Tree Should Not Blossom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet's body shakes at what he has heard, yet he will quietly wait (v. 16). Then the great confession: Though the fig tree should not blossom, and every crop and flock fail, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation (vv. 17-18). GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer's (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Faith's final word is joy in God himself, which survives when every visible support is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver at the sound; rottenness enters into my bones; my legs tremble beneath me. Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us. Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver at the sound; rottenness enters into my bones; my legs tremble beneath me. Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us.

Do not miss what kind of faith this is. Habakkuk is not calm because he has stopped feeling anything. Read the symptoms: my body trembles, my lips quiver, rottenness enters into my bones, my legs tremble. He is physically shaking with dread at the invasion he knows is coming.

And in that state he says, Yet I will quietly wait. Faith is not the absence of fear. It is trusting God while afraid.

Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,

Now comes one of the great sentences of the Bible, and it is built like a staircase going down. Count what is removed: no blossom on the fig tree, no fruit on the vines, no olives, no grain in the fields, no sheep in the fold, no cattle in the stalls.

For a farming community these six clauses are not poetry; they are starvation. Fig, vine and olive were the staple crops; flocks and herds were the savings account. Habakkuk is imagining the total failure of everything that keeps a family alive, which is exactly what an invading army leaves behind.

Notice that he does not deny any of it. He does not say the fig tree will blossom after all. He faces the worst honestly and then speaks the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation. GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer's; he makes me tread on my high places. To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.

Yet. Everything hangs on that word. The barns are empty, the fields are bare, and the sentence turns.

See carefully where the joy is: in the LORD, in the God of my salvation. Not in the harvest, not in an improvement he expects next season, not even in the promise that the Babylonians will one day fall, though that promise is true. His joy has moved from God's gifts to God himself, and that is the one joy that cannot be taken by an invading army.

This is the answer to the question Habakkuk asked in chapter 1. He never does get a full explanation of why God uses wicked nations, and neither will we get explanations for much of what we go through. What he gets is God, and it turns out to be enough.

Paul learned the same lesson: I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content, in plenty and hunger, abundance and need (Phil 4:11-12). Note the word learned. This is not a temperament; it is a discipline, and this chapter shows how it is learned: remember what God has done, look honestly at what may come, and put your joy where it cannot be reached.

GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer's; he makes me tread on my high places. To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments.

The final picture is of a deer on a mountainside. Anyone who has watched one knows the astonishing surefootedness, running along rock ledges where a man would fall. God makes me tread on my high places: not removing the heights, but giving feet for them. David sang the same line (Ps 18:33).

And the book that began with O LORD, how long shall I cry for help ends with a note for the worship leader: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "my stringed"). The complaint has become a hymn.

That is the journey Habakkuk offers to anyone who will take it. Bring God your hardest questions. Wait for his answer. Learn that the righteous live by faith. And find, when everything that can be shaken is shaken, that joy in God himself is still standing.

3.title: Yet I Will Rejoice in the LORD
3.overview:
A prayer of Habakkuk, set to music. He has heard the report of God's work and fears it, and prays that God would revive his work in the midst of the years, make it known, and in wrath remember mercy (vv. 1-2).

Then he sees God coming from Teman and Mount Paran: his splendour covers the heavens, rays flash from his hand, pestilence and plague attend him, the eternal mountains scatter, and the tents of Cushan and Midian tremble (vv. 3-7). Was his anger against the rivers and the sea, or was he riding his chariot of salvation? Mountains writhe, the deep lifts its hands, sun and moon stand still at the flash of his arrows (vv. 8-11). He marches through the earth threshing the nations, going out for the salvation of his people and of his anointed, crushing the head of the house of the wicked and trampling the sea with his horses (vv. 12-15).

The prophet's body trembles at what he has heard, yet he will quietly wait for the day of trouble (v. 16). Though the fig tree does not blossom, the vines bear nothing, the olive fails, the fields yield no food and flock and herd are gone, yet he will rejoice in the LORD and take joy in the God of his salvation (vv. 17-18). GOD, the Lord, is his strength, who makes his feet like the deer's and lets him tread on the heights (v. 19).
3.theology:
Honest wrestling with God can become public worship; Scripture sanctifies lament by setting it to music (v. 1).

The right prayer under judgment is that God would act again as he has acted before, and remember mercy in the midst of wrath (v. 2).

Remembering what God has done is the believer's resource when he cannot see what God is doing (vv. 3-7).

God's displays of power are not temper but purpose: he rides a chariot of salvation (v. 8).

God acts in history for the rescue of his people through his anointed, crushing the head of the enemy as promised in Eden (vv. 13; Gen 3:15).

Faith is not the absence of fear but trust in God while trembling (v. 16).

Joy that rests on God himself, rather than on his gifts, survives the loss of everything (vv. 17-18; Phil 4:11-13).

God does not remove the heights but gives feet for them (v. 19; Ps 18:33).
3.examples:
A private argument with God turned into a hymn for the congregation.

A prayer that asks for mercy inside the judgment, not instead of it.

Light so bright that it is called God veiling his power.

Everlasting hills that turn out not to be everlasting.

A sea split open, not because God was angry with water.

A believer shaking from head to foot and saying "yet".

Six empty things counted, and joy still standing.

A deer running along a ledge where a man would fall.
